messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 54
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Civil Servant
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 59

He is a 54-year-old European man who works as a civil servant and has spent much of his adult life trying to appear steady, reasonable, and unaffected by conflict. He is in a relationship now, but his current capacity for closeness is shaped by a past he rarely talks about directly. The trauma centers on a romantic partnership that began, in his telling, with warmth and ordinary hope. He describes himself at that time as eager to be understood, relieved to have found someone attentive and charming, someone who seemed to admire his calmness. The abuse did not arrive all at once. It began with sharp words, humiliation in private, the sense that he was always doing something wrong. Over time, the criticism became physical: grabbing, shoving, blocking doorways, striking him during arguments, and once leaving him shaken and ashamed after an attack that made him realize he was afraid in his own home.

He says the hardest part was not only the pain, but the disorientation. He kept telling himself it was a phase, that he must be provoking these reactions, that good men did not get trapped in situations like this. He became quieter and more careful, choosing his words with increasing precision. He learned the posture of avoiding danger before it arrived. He watched faces closely, reading shifts in tone, trying to anticipate what might set the other person off. At work, where he was expected to be composed and dependable, he became even more disciplined. He arrived early, stayed late, and buried himself in administrative tasks because structure felt safer than home. Colleagues saw a diligent man who did not complain. They did not see the dread that accompanied the drive back in the evening, or the way he would sit in his car for several minutes before going inside.

The relationship ended, but the violence did not end cleanly in his mind. He carried the events with him as if they were unfinished. In the months that followed, he began sleeping poorly, waking at night with his heart racing, certain for a moment that someone was in the room. He startles easily when a door slams or a voice rises behind him. He has vivid memories that intrude without warning: a hand on his arm, a wall at his back, the sensation of being trapped. At times he replays conversations from that period, hearing again the insult, the accusation, the abrupt change from charm to rage. He tries to make sense of where he could have acted differently, returning again and again to the hope that if he can understand it, he can prevent it from happening again.

Even now, he remains guarded in relationships. He is in a current partnership that is gentler, but he notices how quickly his body braces when there is tension. A delayed text can set off a chain of thoughts about rejection or danger. If his partner speaks sharply, even for a moment, he feels the old tightening in his chest and the urge to withdraw. He often says “it’s fine” when it is not fine, because conflict feels like a doorway he does not want to open. He is embarrassed by how easily he becomes hypervigilant, checking tone, scanning for signs that an ordinary disagreement could turn threatening. Intimacy brings both comfort and fear; at times he wants closeness desperately, and at other times he feels strangely distant, as if part of him is standing outside the room watching for what might go wrong.

He notices changes in himself in smaller ways as well. He is more irritable than he used to be, though he works hard not to show it. He avoids places, songs, and conversations that remind him of the abusive relationship, and when reminders appear unexpectedly he can feel abruptly unsettled for hours. Some evenings he sits in silence after work, too drained to read or watch television, wanting only to get through the day without being pulled backward. At other times he forces himself to keep moving, doing chores or tidying the kitchen in a deliberate, almost mechanical way, as if order can hold off the memories.

There is a dignity in the way he speaks about what happened, but also a persistent sadness beneath it. He has spent years minimizing the impact, telling himself that others have endured worse, that he should have recovered by now. In session, he begins to acknowledge that the abuse changed how he experiences safety, trust, and his own body. What he describes is not only the memory of being hurt, but the long afterlife of that hurt in ordinary moments: in sleep, in arguments, in the pause before answering a message, in the way he listens for danger even when none is immediately present.
